notes: Scope: FLEX (PSI-69), FLEX-2 (PSI-68) and CFI (PSI-39), all run with the Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) in the Combustion Integrated Rack on the ISS. FLEX-2J and FLEX-ICE-GA used the same hardware (NASA fact sheet, raw/nasa/flex.txt) but have no PSI record under those names and are not covered here.

Sources used: PSI records and per-test tables (raw/psi), PSI-hosted documents fetched for this file (raw/pdf/PSI-39_*, PSI-68_*, PSI-69_*), NTRS abstracts (raw/ntrs) and NTRS full texts (raw/pdf/<id>.txt), NASA pages and the Researcher's Guide (raw/nasa). Fetch log: raw/pdf/_fetchlog_droplets.jsonl. This file is written by raw/pdf/_droplets_tools/build_droplets.py (run with python3; it cuts every quote from the cached text and drops any it cannot verify).

NTRS 20150023456 (NASA/TP-2015-216046): the PDF is 42,900,650 bytes, over the 20 MB limit, so it was not downloaded. raw/pdf/20150023456.txt is the full text that NTRS itself serves (downloads[].links.fulltext). That text joins some words across line breaks (for example "hydroxylfilter"); quotes keep it as it is.
NTRS 20120015928 and 20120016855: PDFs saved, but they are scans from which pdftotext extracts nothing, and the NTRS full-text links return 0 bytes. Only their abstracts (raw/ntrs) are used.

NTRS records found by new searches and not in ntrs-index.json: 20140006750, 20150018397, 20170000666, 20190002838, 20205008449. For each, raw/pdf/<id>.record.json is the API record, raw/pdf/<id>.abstract.txt is title + blank line + abstract (same layout as raw/ntrs/<id>.txt) and raw/pdf/<id>.pdf / .txt is the full text. Findings with source.kind "ntrs" that point to raw/pdf/<id>.abstract.txt quote the abstract.
Quotes are cut from the text files by script; line-break hyphens of PDF text are kept (for example "tech- nology", "fun- damental"), as are ligatures and curly quotes.

Attribution of n-octane and n-decane results to FLEX-2: the 2014 paper (20140006750) calls all ISS droplet tests "FLEX experiments". They are filed under FLEX-2 here because the PSI-68 table lists n-Octane and Decane while the PSI-69 table lists only Methanol and Heptane. Findings from sources that pool FLEX, FLEX-2 and CFI data (20205008449, 20210022617) are filed under the investigation whose question they answer.

Background figures in the FLEX test plan (Takahashi et al. 2004, Katta et al. 2004, Honda and Ronney 1998) are results of other studies that the FLEX team cites to justify the experiment; they are marked "background cited in the FLEX test plan" in the topic and are not FLEX measurements.

DROPLETS findings quoting a row of a PSI CSV table restate one test record; column meanings come from the header row of the same file (for PSI-69: test number, identifier, date, GMT, fuel, pressure in mmHg, O, N, CO, He mole fractions, initial diameter mm, visible flame extinction diameter mm, burning rate, burn time s, test end). The PSI headers print "O", "N", "CO" for oxygen, nitrogen and carbon dioxide.
The finding on precursor CO2 tests (NTRS 20110020695) is labelled ground low-gravity because the abstract calls the experiments precursors to the ISS runs; the abstract does not name the facility.

The FLEX-2 droplet-array findings from the science requirements document describe precursor low-gravity tests cited there (the document says ground-based facilities limited them); the fuel is not named in the quoted passage, so "fuel" is null.

Suppressants: the PSI-69 record names CO2, He and SF6 and the Researcher's Guide names xenon; the PSI-69 test table holds only CO2 and He columns, and the NASA fact sheet says "The suppressants are carbon dioxide and helium." No SF6 result was found in the saved sources.
Dates: PSI investigation start/end dates do not match flight operations (CFI flew in 2017 but PSI lists 2020-2021; FLEX-2 lists 2016-2019). Both are recorded in "years" with their quotes.

CFI final report wording: section 5.1 writes "n-dodecanol" and "iso-dodecanol" where the fuels flown were n-dodecane and iso-dodecane, and the caption of its Figure 3 gives a gas mixture that does not add to 100%. The quote is kept verbatim and the Figure 3 values are not used.
Test FLEX-377 (n-decane, 0.5 atm) is given as air in the 2021 presentation and as 25% oxygen in the 2015 presentation; no finding relies on its oxygen value.

Not found in the saved sources for this family: smoke particle sizes or detector response measurements (those belong to SAME/SAME-R), flame spread rates (single droplets do not spread; FLEX-2J droplet-array spread has no PSI record), and any partial-gravity droplet data.

Finding on the CO2-triggered cool flame model (source PSI-69_Presentation-1G17-070HE-0166): the quote contains a stray "5" between "An increase" and "in the CO2"; it is the page number, which sits inside that sentence in the PDF text.
The quote for the three n-heptane cases (20140006750) starts at "shows three typical" because the words "Figure 3" are split from it by a page break in the PDF text.

The decane/hexanol finding (20170000666): the NASA fact sheet names n-hexanol/n-decane as a FLEX-ICE-GA fuel, flown "in the FLEX-2 configuration"; it is filed under FLEX-2 because the PSI-68 record lists the decane/hexanol paper among its publications.
evidence_level is "review or summary" where the quoted sentence is a NASA summary, rationale or cited background, even when the underlying work was a flight experiment.
earth_instinct and decision_hint are interpretation written for VESTA, not NASA statements.

investigations.hardware: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) inside the chamber of the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), part of the Fluids and Combustion Facility (FCF)

investigations.pi: Forman A. Williams, University of California, San Diego
investigations.objectives: Map the flammability limits of liquid fuel droplets in microgravity, in particular the limiting oxygen index (LOI) as a function of pressure; measure the effectiveness of gaseous fire suppressants (CO2, He and SF6 are named in the PSI record; the PSI test table holds CO2 and He tests); provide data for predictive models of combustion limits.
investigations.sample_geometry: Single liquid fuel droplets with initial diameters between 2 and 5 mm (PSI test table: 1.1 to 4.67 mm), deployed free-floating or supported on a fiber in a quiescent chamber atmosphere

conditions.o2_percent: 12 to 34 (oxygen mole fraction 0.12 to 0.34 in the PSI test table)
conditions.pressure: 0.70 to 3.05 atm; most tests between 0.7 and 1 atm
conditions.flow: Quiescent; in some tests a fiber-supported droplet was translated at about 3 mm/s to impose a slow, sub-buoyant flow

investigations.variables: Varied from test to test: fuel (methanol or heptane), ambient oxygen mole fraction, diluent or suppressant gas and its mole fraction (nitrogen, carbon dioxide up to 0.70, helium up to 0.45 in the PSI test table), ambient pressure, initial droplet diameter, free or fiber-supported droplet, quiescent or slowly translated. Held the same: single droplet geometry, hot-wire ignition, ambient temperature, the CIR/MDCA hardware and cameras.
measurements: Droplet diameter history from a backlit camera (HiBMs)
Flame diameter history from a low-light UV camera filtered for OH chemiluminescence at 310 nm (LLUV) and from a color camera
Average burning-rate constant and extinction droplet diameter for each burn
Flame size, shape and color overview from the MDCA color camera (downlinked during operations)
Broadband and water-vapor-band radiometers (not sensitive enough to give reliable quantitative data in the tests of the 2015 report)

findings.topic: Why carbon dioxide can behave differently without buoyancy
findings.claim: The FLEX test plan explains that without buoyantly-driven convective flows, radiative losses can become a significant fraction of the heat loss from the reaction zone, and that when a thermally participating gas such as CO2 limits radiative exchange between flame and ambient, temperatures near the fuel source will increase.

findings.topic: Fuel keeps reacting after the visible flame is gone
findings.claim: In FLEX, large alkane droplets burned briefly with a typical hot flame that extinguished when radiative loss lowered the flame temperature; after that the droplet continued to vaporize at the same rate for an extended period and then suddenly stopped at a finite size, with a large vapor cloud forming; this vaporization is supported by a lower-temperature cool flame that forms after visible flame extinction.
findings.quote: Recent spaceflight experiments (FLEX) involving single alkane droplets burning in a quiescent ambient uncovered unexplained and unexpected behavior. For the large alkane droplets, after ignition the droplet burns for a short time with a typical hot flame. As expected, the hot flame extinguished when the radiative loss reduced the flame temperature below a critical value. Inexplicably after hot flame extinction, however, the droplet continued to vaporize at the same rate for an extended period and then suddenly stopped vaporizing at a finite droplet size. The plateau in vaporization occurred coincident with the formation of a large vapor cloud. This vaporization, we now know, is supported by a lower-temperature cool flame that forms after visible flame extinction.

findings.claim: In FLEX test 035 (free-floating heptane droplet, cabin air, 1.0 atm), after the visible flame extinguished the droplet vaporized very vigorously at a rate only slightly lower than the burning rate constant before extinction, then the rate plateaued as a very large vapor cloud formed; the report calls this indicative of cool flame burning and extinction.
findings.quote: Figure 39.—Test FLEX−035. Free-floating heptane droplet in a cabin air (0.21/0.79 O2/N2), 1.0-atm ambient environment. The droplet remained in the High-Bit-Depth Multispectral (HiBMs) field of view (FOV) for the entire test including a long time after the visible flame extinguished. The flame oscillated before the visible flame extinguished, and this was apparent in both the Low Light Level Ultra-Violet (LLUV) and color camera. After the flame extinguished, the droplet vaporized very vigorously with droplet-diameter-squared versus time behavior that was nearly perfectly linear. The vaporization rate was only slightly lower than the burning rate constant before the flame extinguished. The droplet vaporization rate then plateaued coincident with the formation of a very large vapor cloud. This behavior is indicative of cool flame burning and extinction.

findings.topic: Model: flash re-ignition after about 18 s of cool flame
findings.claim: A two-dimensional simulation of the FLEX observations with a gaseous n-heptane source in zero gravity found that in near-quiescent air (2 mm/s or less) the growing spherical flame extinguishes at about 1200 K from radiative heat loss, moves to a cool-flame regime with a reaction zone at about 700 K close to the fuel source, and after about 18 s of cool flame a flash re-ignition occurs.
findings.quote: In a near-quiescent air environment (< or = 2 mm/s), with a sufficiently large fuel injection velocity (1 cm/s), a growing spherical diffusion flame extinguishes at ≈1200 K due to radiative heat losses. This is typically followed by a transition to the low-temperature (cool-flame) regime with a reaction zone (at ≈700 K) in close proximity to the fuel source. The 'cool flame' regime is formed due to the negative temperature coefficient in the low-temperature chemistry. After a relatively long period (≈18 s) of the cool flame regime, a flash re-ignition occurs, associated with flame-edge propagation and subsequent extinction of the re-ignited flame.

source.title: Combustion Characteristics in a Non-Premixed Cool-Flame Regime of n-Heptane in Microgravity

findings.earth_instinct: Once a fire is out, it stays out unless something lights it again.
findings.decision_hint: Expect a possible flash back to a hot flame some tens of seconds after flame-out in still air; keep crew and extinguisher positioned for it.

findings.topic: Model: millimetre-per-second airflow changes whether the flame survives
findings.claim: In the same simulation, a low-speed airstream of about 3 mm/s enhanced the diffusion flame upstream with local extinction downstream and steady pulsations at about 0.4 Hz, and at air velocities of 4 to 10 mm/s the locally extinguished flame became steady.
findings.quote: In a low-speed (≈3 mm/s) airstream (which simulates the slight droplet movement), the diffusion flame is enhanced upstream and experiences a local extinction downstream at ≈1200 K, followed by steady flame pulsations (≈0.4 Hz). At higher air velocities (4-10 mm/s), the locally extinguished flame becomes steady state.

findings.earth_instinct: Air that barely moves cannot matter to a flame.
findings.decision_hint: After fans are shut off, residual air motion of a few mm/s can be enough to hold a flame on its upstream side; allow the flow to decay and check where the residual flow comes from.

findings.topic: Flame went out when a 3 mm/s flow stopped (single test)
findings.claim: In FLEX test 064 a fiber-supported heptane droplet in 0.18/0.82 O2/N2 at 1.0 atm was translated at 3 mm/s for about 4 s: during translation the leading edge of the flame was bright and the trailing edge much dimmer; after translation stopped the flame extinguished and the droplet vaporized significantly, behavior the report calls indicative of cool flame burning and extinction.
findings.quote: Figure 68.—Test FLEX−064. Fiber-supported heptane droplet translating 3 mm/s (for approximately 4 s) and burning in a 0.18/0.82 O2/N2, 1.0-atm ambient environment. The droplet had moderate transverse oscillations and remained within the High-Bit-Depth Multispectral (HiBMs) field of view (FOV) for the entire test. The flame grew and became dim blue. During translation, the leading edge of the flame was bright and the fiber glowed brightly. The trailing edge of the flame was much dimmer and the fiber did not glow. After the translation stopped, the flame extinguished and the droplet vaporized significantly. A small disruption very late in the droplet lifetime left a small residual droplet on the fiber. The behavior after the visible flame extinguished is indicative of cool flame burning and extinction.

source.title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011 (NASA/TP-2015-216046)

conditions.flow: 3 mm/s for approximately 4 s, then none

findings.earth_instinct: Air that barely moves cannot matter to a flame.
findings.decision_hint: Stopping the airflow ended the visible flame in this single test at 18% oxygen, which supports fan shutdown as a first step, but fuel kept reacting afterwards: follow fan shutdown with a non-visual check.

findings.topic: Precursor tests: carbon dioxide at fixed 21% oxygen barely changed methanol extinction
findings.claim: In precursor microgravity experiments (before the ISS runs) with 1.25 to 1.72 mm methanol droplets at one atmosphere and oxygen fixed at 21%, the extinction diameter grew with initial droplet diameter, while increasing the carbon dioxide concentration led only to a slight decrease in the extinction diameter.
findings.quote: Diffusive extinction of methanol droplets with initial diameters between 1.25 mm and 1.72 mm, burning in a quiescent microgravity environment at one atmosphere pressure, was obtained experimentally for varying levels of ambient carbon-dioxide concentrations with a fixed oxygen concentration of 21% and a balance of nitrogen. These experiments serve as precursors to those which are beginning to be performed on the International Space Station and are motivated by the need to understand the effectiveness of carbon-dioxide as a fire suppressant in low-gravity environments. In these experiments, the flame standoff distance, droplet diameter, and flame radiation are measured as functions of time. The results show that the droplet extinction diameter depends on both the initial droplet diameter and the ambient concentration of carbon dioxide. Increasing the initial droplet diameter leads to an increased extinction diameter, while increasing the carbon-dioxide concentration leads to a slight decrease in the extinction diameter.

source.title: Methanol Droplet Extinction in Carbon-Dioxide-Enriched Environments in Microgravity

findings.earth_instinct: Flood a fire with carbon dioxide and it goes out.
findings.decision_hint: Adding CO2 without lowering the oxygen fraction did not make these small flames go out sooner; a suppressant plan has to displace oxygen.

findings.topic: An atmosphere that does not burn in normal gravity burned in microgravity
findings.claim: Precursor tests described in the FLEX-2 science requirements: in 0.15 oxygen mole fraction (balance nitrogen) at 190 mmHg, a single droplet burned to completion in microgravity although that ambient was not flammable in normal gravity, where droplets of this size could not sustain a flame at this oxygen fraction at pressures up to 760 mmHg; the flame around a binary array extinguished about one second after the igniter withdrew.
findings.quote: Figure 8 shows the burning behavior for a single droplet and a binary array (L ≈ 3 mm) in a 0.15 oxygen mole fraction (balance nitrogen), 190 mmHg ambient. There are several noteworthy features of the single droplet burning behavior. First, this ambient condition was not ﬂammable in normal gravity. In fact, in this ambient oxygen mole fraction, droplets of this size could not sustain a ﬂame in normal gravity at pressures up to 760 mmHg. Figure 8 also shows that while the single droplet burned to completion, the ﬂame surrounding the array extinguished approximately one second after the igniter withdrew.

findings.earth_instinct: If it will not burn in this atmosphere on the ground, it will not burn in space.
findings.decision_hint: A low-pressure, low-oxygen atmosphere that passes a normal-gravity flammability test can still burn in microgravity; qualify exploration atmospheres with low-gravity data.

findings.topic: Two neighbouring droplets extinguished earlier than one in nitrogen-diluted 15% oxygen
findings.claim: In the 0.15 oxygen mole fraction ambient, over a range of inter-droplet spacings and ambient pressures, the flame surrounding a binary droplet array always extinguished at a finite droplet size larger than the single droplet extinction diameter.
findings.quote: The above trends were consistent over a range of inter-droplet spacings and ambient pressures. In the 0.15 oxygen mole fraction ambient, the ﬂame surrounding the binary array always extinguished at a ﬁnite droplet size that was larger than the single droplet extinction diameter.

findings.earth_instinct: More fuel close together always burns better.
findings.decision_hint: Near the oxygen limit in nitrogen-diluted air, a merged flame around neighbouring fuel elements loses more heat by radiation and can go out sooner; do not extrapolate single-item limits to clustered fuel in either direction.

findings.topic: In helium-diluted oxygen the trend reverses: the pair burned longer
findings.claim: In an oxygen/helium ambient the flame around a single droplet extinguished quickly after ignition (extinction diameter about 1.4 mm) while the flame around the binary array burned much longer to a smaller extinction diameter (about 1.1 mm), a trend opposite to the O2/N2 experiments but in agreement with normal gravity experiments.
findings.quote: The ﬂame surrounding the single droplet extinguishes quickly after ignition (Dext ≈ 1.4 mm). The ﬂame surrounding the binary array, however, burns much longer, and the extinction droplet diameter is much smaller (Dext ≈ 1.1 mm). This extinction trend is opposite to that displayed in O2 /N2 experiments, but in agreement with the normal gravity experiments.

findings.claim: For n-decane droplets of similar size burning in 17% O2 / 83% N2 at 1 atm, single droplets showed only a hot flame while binary droplets showed a cool flame.

findings.decision_hint: Clustered fuel can enter the invisible cool-flame mode under conditions where an isolated item does not; assume the less visible outcome when several fuel sources are close together.

findings.topic: Cameras saw nothing during the cool flame; radiometers did
findings.claim: During the second, cool-flame stage of an n-decane droplet burn, neither the color camera nor the UV camera was sensitive enough to register any flame image, while both the broadband and narrowband radiometers registered continued radiative heat loss from the droplet, indicating active chemical heat release.
findings.quote: Both the color camera and the UV-camera are not sensitive enough to register any ﬂame images during this period. Both the broadband and narrowband radiometers, however, register continued radiative heat loss from the droplet indicating active chemical heat release.

findings.decision_hint: Pair optical flame detection with infrared radiometry or gas sensing; in this test only the radiometers showed that reaction was continuing.

findings.topic: Burning rate in the invisible stage about four fifths of the visible stage
findings.claim: ISS test R298 (n-octane series, droplet of 3.6 mm burning in air): both hot-flame and cool-flame burning modes existed, with burning rates of 0.48 and 0.38 mm2/s respectively.
findings.quote: Test R298 results shown in Fig. (2a) corresponds to a droplet with D0 = 3.6 mm burning in air (O2 :N2 = 0.21:0.79) with no helium dilution. Both hot-ﬂame and cool-ﬂame burning modes were found to exist with the respective burning rates of 0.48 and 0.38 mm2 /s.

findings.earth_instinct: When you can no longer see a flame, the fire is out.
findings.decision_hint: Fuel was consumed in the cool-flame stage at 0.38 against 0.48 mm2/s for the hot flame; absence of a visible flame is not evidence that fuel consumption has stopped.

findings.topic: Lower oxygen brought earlier hot-flame and cool-flame extinction
findings.claim: For n-decane droplets at 0.5 atm in oxygen/nitrogen mixtures, reducing the ambient oxygen concentration led to earlier hot and cool flame extinctions.
findings.quote: In general it can be summarized based on the results presented in Fig. 1 that reducing the ambient oxygen concentration leads to earlier hot and cool ﬂame extinctions.

findings.decision_hint: Lowering oxygen shortens both stages; an oxygen draw-down is still a valid response, provided the invisible stage is monitored.

findings.topic: Higher oxygen removed radiative self-extinction
findings.claim: When the oxygen concentration was sufficiently high, radiative extinction was avoided and visible flame extinction occurred at a much smaller droplet size, either by micro-explosion of the droplet or by diffusive extinction.
findings.quote: When the oxygen concentration is sufﬁciently high radiative extinction is avoided and visible ﬂame extinction occurs at a much smaller droplet size either by micro-explosion of the droplet or by diffusive extinction.

findings.decision_hint: In oxygen-enriched exploration atmospheres do not count on a large fuel source putting itself out by radiative loss; the same paper reports a 25% oxygen, 0.5 atm case that burned until the droplet micro-exploded 26 seconds after ignition.

findings.topic: 75% helium: hot flame died in a fraction of a second, brief cool flame followed
findings.claim: In ISS test R707 (n-octane series, oxygen mole fraction 0.21, helium dilution 75% by volume, droplet of 2.49 mm) first-stage burning was almost eliminated: the hot flame formed at ignition died within a fraction of a second, cool flame burning began immediately and also ended quickly, leaving the droplet to evaporate.
findings.quote: When helium dilution was increased to 75% by volume in test R707 for D0 of 2.49 mm ﬁrst stage burning is almost eliminated (see, Fig. (2d)). The hot ﬂame that formed during the ignition dies within a fraction of a second and the cool ﬂame burning commences immediately which also ends quickly leaving the droplet to evaporate.

findings.decision_hint: Heavy helium dilution removed the hot flame almost at once in this test, yet a short cool flame still occurred; 75% helium with 21% oxygen is a test atmosphere, not a cabin setting.

findings.topic: After extinction, n-octane still lost mass faster than by evaporation alone
findings.claim: For an n-octane droplet of 3.61 mm initial diameter, the burning rate dropped at extinction, but the post-extinction burning rate was still higher than the rate of pure evaporation.
findings.quote: Figures 9a, 9d and 9e show such a decrease for n-octane with Do = 3.61 mm at about 1.0 s/mm2. At larger times the octane burning rate is much lower, though the post-extinction burning rate is still higher than the rate of pure evaporation for n-octane as shown by the green data in Fig. 9a.

findings.earth_instinct: When you can no longer see a flame, the fire is out.
findings.decision_hint: Fuel loss faster than plain evaporation after flame-out is a usable sign that reaction continues; a mass-loss or vapor measurement can stand in for a flame sensor.

findings.topic: Larger droplets burned dimmer and with less soot
findings.claim: For initial droplet diameters above 1.5 mm, n-octane and n-decane droplet flames appeared less luminous and therefore less sooty, yet the droplets burned progressively slower as initial diameter increased.
findings.quote: For Do > 1.5 mm the droplet flames appeared less luminous and therefore less sooty, yet the droplets continued to burn progressively slower as Do increased.

findings.earth_instinct: A bigger fire is brighter and smokier, so easier to detect.
findings.decision_hint: Larger, radiatively cooled flames in these tests gave less light and less soot; a detector that depends on soot particles or brightness has less to work with as the fuel source grows.

findings.topic: Fire sensing in microgravity relies on particle scattering
findings.claim: The FLEX-2 science requirements note that understanding soot formation matters for fire safety because fire sensing technology in microgravity environments typically relies on scattering from particles.
findings.quote: Understanding soot formation is also important in ﬁre safety applications. Fire sensing tech- nology in microgravity environments typically relies on scattering from particles(Urban et al. (1997)).

findings.claim: FLEX is focused on spacecraft fire safety and fire suppression, while FLEX-2 returns to the broader objective of improving the fundamental understanding of liquid-fuel combustion.
findings.quote: While FLEX is focussed on spacecraft ﬁre safety and ﬁre suppression, FLEX-2 returns to the broader objective of improving the fun- damental understanding of liquid-fuel combustion.

findings.decision_hint: Rank FLEX above FLEX-2 for suppressant and oxygen-limit questions; use FLEX-2 for fuel mixtures, soot, slow flow and droplet-pair effects.

findings.topic: Fuel mixture at elevated pressure: very weak visible flame, high burning rate
findings.claim: Experiments with large bi-component droplets (n-decane and hexanol, 50/50 by volume) at elevated pressures showed the visible hot flame becoming extremely weak while the burning rate remained relatively high, with radiant output too high to be accounted for by a visible hot flame alone.
findings.quote: Recent experiments involving large, bi-component fuel (n-decane and hexanol, 50/50 by volume) droplets at elevated pressures show that the visible, hot flame becomes extremely weak while the burning rate remains relatively high, suggesting the possibility of simultaneous presence of "cool" and "hot" flames of roughly equal importance. The radiant output from these bi-component droplets is relatively high and cannot be accounted for only by the presence of a visible hot-flame.

findings.earth_instinct: A weak-looking flame is a weak fire.
findings.decision_hint: Flame brightness did not track burning rate for this fuel mixture; size the response from heat or fuel-loss signals rather than from how the flame looks.

findings.topic: Repeated re-ignition cycles above 2 atm
findings.claim: In CFI, as ambient pressure was increased above 2 atm, multiple reignition cycles were observed: the hot flame extinguished by radiative heat loss, a cool flame followed, then reignition to a hot flame followed by a cool flame, the cycle repeating several times until the fuel droplet was completely consumed.
findings.quote: No new anomalies or surprises were observed during the CFI experiments. However, as the ambient pressure is increased above 2 atm, multiple reignition cycles were observed, where first the hot flame extinguishes due to radiative heat loss followed by cool flame, and then reignition to a hot-flame followed by a cool flame, with this cycle repeating several times until the fuel droplet is completely consumed.

findings.decision_hint: Direct evidence that a liquid-fuel flame can relight itself several times with no new ignition source. The cycles were seen above 2 atm, higher than cabin pressures, so treat it as proof of mechanism rather than a prediction for a 1 atm or lower habitat.

findings.topic: Warm flames were not visible in the color camera
findings.claim: In CFI, warm flames were observed typically at higher pressures following radiative extinction and were not visible in the color camera; subsequently a hot flame ignited and quickly extinguished to form a cool flame.
findings.quote: Warm flames were observed typically at higher pressures following radiative extinction and the flame is not visible in the color camera. Subsequently, a hot flame is ignited which quickly extinguishes to form a cool flame.

findings.topic: Branched fuel component reduced the tendency to form cool flames
findings.claim: The CFI final report states that cool flames were observed for the pure fuel and for the fuel mixtures, and that adding the iso component reduced the tendency to form cool flames (the report writes "n-dodecanol" and "iso-dodecanol" in this passage; the fuels flown were n-dodecane and n-dodecane/iso-dodecane mixtures).
findings.quote: Cool flames were observed during n-dodecanol combustion as well as n-dodecanol/iso-dodecanol mixture cases. The addition of iso-dodecanol reduces the tendency to form cool flames in n-dodecanol.

findings.decision_hint: Cool-flame tendency depends on fuel structure: straight-chain hydrocarbons are the worst case in this data, so fluids rich in normal alkanes deserve the most caution.

findings.topic: No soot from the cool flame at low pressure; residual soot at higher pressure
findings.claim: In CFI, at low pressures soot is not formed in the cool flame because of its low flame temperature, and soot formed during the hot flame is simply convected away from the droplet surface; when the pressure increases, residual soot is seen surrounding the droplet even after hot flame extinction.
findings.quote: At low pressures, due to the low flame temperature of the cool flame, soot is not formed. The soot that is formed during the hot flame combustion is simply convected away from the droplet surface. But, when the pressure increases, residual soot is seen surrounding the droplet even after the hot flame extinction.

findings.decision_hint: At the lower pressures tested the cool flame made no soot of its own, so a particle-scattering smoke detector should not be the only watch after flame-out.

findings.claim: The CFI final report gives as rationale for microgravity that cool flames need much longer residence times and cannot be observed under normal gravity conditions with droplet flames.
findings.quote: Moreover, the cool flames need much longer residence times and cannot be observed under normal gravity conditions with droplet flames.

findings.decision_hint: Ground flammability testing cannot screen for this mode; label it "not testable in 1-g" in a hazard analysis and "never tested" for lunar and Martian gravity.

findings.topic: A vapor cloud of condensed, partly oxidized fuel marks the end of the cool flame
findings.claim: When the cool-flame stage ended, a vapor cloud formed around the droplet as partially oxidized fuel condensed immediately following cool-flame extinction.
findings.quote: A vapor cloud was also found to form around the droplet as the partially oxidized fuel condensed immediately following cool-flame extinction.

findings.claim: The CFI final report states that all the CFI data is yet to be fully analyzed and interpreted using theoretical and numerical models.

findings.claim: The FLEX team concludes that existing, widely used detailed chemical kinetic models do not accurately predict the second-stage cool flame extinction (and warm flame) and need further improvement.

findings.earth_instinct: A validated combustion model will predict when the fire is over.
findings.decision_hint: Do not let a simulation decide when a liquid-fuel fire has ended; the low-temperature stage is where today's models are weakest.

findings.topic: Inert gas choice changes cool-flame extinction: helium ends it early, xenon prolongs it
findings.claim: ISS droplet experiments in which some of the ambient nitrogen was replaced by carbon dioxide, helium or xenon show that different diluents act very differently on cool-flame combustion: the cool-flame extinction diameter is drastically increased with helium dilution compared to N2, CO2 or Xe, and that Xe dilution leads to longer burning with a smaller extinction diameter.
findings.quote: In these ISS experiments, some of the nitrogen in the ambient gas mixture is replaced by an inert gas, namely, carbon dioxide, helium, or xenon. Different diluents were observed to exert remarkably different influences on the cool-flame combustion of fuel droplets. The results show that the cool-flame extinction diameter is drastically increased with helium dilution compared to N2, CO2 or Xe, and Xe dilution leads to longer burning with a smaller extinction diameter.

findings.decision_hint: Against the invisible stage the diluents are not equivalent: helium cut the cool flame short far more than nitrogen, CO2 or xenon did, and xenon let it burn longer.

findings.claim: The same study concludes that xenon decreases burning rates substantially but can sustain cool flames at much lower oxygen concentrations compared to helium.
findings.quote: Xenon decreases burning rates substantially, but can sustain cool flames at much lower oxygen concentrations compared to helium.

findings.topic: Cool flames can extend flammability in microgravity

findings.quote: Cool flames can extend the flammability of fuels in a microgravity environment, and understanding their burning characteristics is important from spacecraft fire safety point of view.

findings.earth_instinct: Once a fire is out, it stays out unless something lights it again.
findings.decision_hint: With the trigger conditions for re-ignition not established, use the conservative protocol after any liquid-fuel fire: keep the area isolated and monitored instead of predicting when it is safe.

findings.topic: Fuels that appear to go out but keep burning
findings.claim: NASA summarizes the Cool Flames Investigation: some types of fuels initially burn very hot, then appear to go out, but they continue burning at a much lower temperature with no visible flames.
findings.quote: Some types of fuels initially burn very hot, then appear to go out — but they continue burning at a much lower temperature with no visible flames, an occurrence called cool flames.

conditions.fuel: pure hydrocarbons, biofuels and mixtures of pure hydrocarbons

findings.earth_instinct: When you can no longer see a flame, the fire is out.
findings.decision_hint: Plain-language rule for crew training: "looks out" is not "is out" for liquid fuels in microgravity.
